  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.

  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *const E::Word`).
  Verus does not support `usize`→pointer casts (int-to-ptr materialization of externally-owned,
  volatile page-table memory), so the body cannot be verified. Same trust-boundary rationale as
  `bump_allocator::alloc` (`usize as *mut`) and `frame::instance`. See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-table/verus-unsupported.md`. **The function is not contract-free:** it
  carries a full `#[verus_spec]` pinned to the global page-table-memory ghost — `requires index@ <
  PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, `ensures result == spec_table_read::<E>(self@.addr, index@)` — exactly as
  `frame::instance` pins its result to `phys_view()` (parameter-free global ghost, no signature
  change).
- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::write` — writes a `TableEntry` into a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *mut E::Word`).

  `requires index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (auto from `TableIndex::inv`); it has **no** contents
  `ensures`. A contents postcondition pinning the *pure* global ghost `spec_table_word(self@.addr,
  index@)` to the caller-chosen `entry` would be unsound for an `external_body` (assumed)
  contract: two writes of distinct entries to the same slot would assume
  `spec_entry_raw(e1) == spec_entry_raw(e2)`, which with `lemma_entry_roundtrip` derives
  `e1 == e2`, i.e. `false` (Turn 2 review #2/#3/#15; exploit reproduced). The genuine `old@ -> @`
  slot-update transition (`self@.entries[index@] == Some(entry)`, other slots framed) is therefore
  **deferred to the proving-phase page-table permission token**, exactly the `identity_map_view()`
  `v -> v'` deferral convention in `identity_map.spec.rs`.

  entry for `vaddr`. Verus does not support inline-asm expressions, so the body cannot be
  verified — an external-bottom hardware trust boundary (same class as the volatile

  `ensures` (returns `()`, no Rust-visible effect, every caller-side invariant preserved).

  `pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::paging::invlpg ](vaddr: usize);` (no
  `requires`/`ensures`). No exec signature changed.

# Caller Analysis: `x86/mem/paging/pde.rs` (Page Directory Entry)

## Script Output
See: `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-arch-x86-pde/find_callers_output.md`

> **Note on script results:** the LSP script reported **0 external callers** for
> every public function. This is a false negative: rust-analyzer indexed the
> `arch` crate in isolation and did not resolve cross-crate references from the
> `kernel` crate (and others). Manual `grep`/`view` across `src/` confirms there
> are many real callers, all of which live in the **`kernel`** crate. The
> analysis below is based on those verified call sites, not on the script's
> empty external-caller list.

## Scope

Verification-order target functions (only these are in scope):

- `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`
- `PageDirectoryEntry::new`
- `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`
- `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::is_present`
- `PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address`

## Where the callers live

| Caller file | Functions used |
|---|---|
| `src/kernel/src/hal/arch/shared/mem/mmu/page_directory.rs` | `PageDirectoryEntry::new`, `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`, `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`, (`from_raw_value`, `into_raw_value`, `frame_number`) |
| `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.rs` | `PageDirectoryEntry::new`, `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`, `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`, `PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address` |
| `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/vmem.rs` | `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present` (via `read_pde`) |
| `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs` | Verus `assume_specification[…]` for all in-scope functions |
| `src/uservm/src/guest_profiler/gva.rs` | `PageDirectoryEntry::SIZE` (const only — not in scope) |

`PageDirectoryEntryFlags::is_present` has **no direct external caller**; it is
reached only internally, through `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`, which
delegates `self.flags.is_present()`. It is in scope because its spec underpins
the spec of `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`.

## Verus Obligation (the primary consumer)

`src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs` declares external specifications
that the kernel's verified code depends on:

```rust
pub assume_specification[ PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new ]( … 8 flag args … ) -> PageDirectoryEntryFlags;
pub assume_specification[ PageDirectoryEntry::new ](flags: PageDirectoryEntryFlags, frame: FrameNumber) -> PageDirectoryEntry;
pub assume_specification[ PageDirectoryEntry::is_present ](pde: &PageDirectoryEntry) -> bool;
pub assume_specification[ PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address ](pde: &PageDirectoryEntry) -> usize;
```

The types are also lifted as opaque (`external_body`) spec types:
`ExPageDirectoryEntry`, `ExPageDirectoryEntryFlags`. This tells us the **View**
should expose the *abstract* properties these specs need (presence, frame
address, the flag values fed into `new`) — not the bit-level encoding.

## Caller Expectations

### `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new(present, read_write, user_supervisor, page_write_through, page_cache_disable, accessed, dirty, page_size)`
- **Callers assume:** the returned flags value faithfully *records each of the 8
  flag arguments*, so that a subsequent query reflects the inputs. In
  particular, callers that pass `PresentFlag::Present`/`NotPresent` expect
  `is_present()` on the resulting PDE to return `true`/`false` accordingly
  (see `page_directory.rs::map`/`unmap`, `identity_map.rs::ensure_pt`).
- It is a pure, total constructor — never fails, no side effects.
- **Callers don't care about:** the internal bit layout, field ordering, or how
  flags are packed into the raw `PteWord`.

### `PageDirectoryEntry::new(flags, frame)`
- **Callers assume:** the returned PDE pairs *these exact* `flags` with *this
  exact* `frame`. Specifically:
  - `is_present()` of the result == `flags.is_present()` (the present bit they
    passed in).
  - `frame_address()` of the result == `frame.into_raw_value() << FRAME_SHIFT`,
    i.e. the physical base address of `frame`.
- Pure, total constructor (no failure, no side effects).
- **Callers don't care about:** raw encoding; they immediately either store it
  via `write_pde`/`pd.write` (round-tripping through `into_raw_value`) or read
  it back through the accessors.

### `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present(&self)`
- **Callers assume:** returns the present bit exactly as set when the PDE was
  constructed / decoded. Used as a guard with strong control-flow meaning:
  - `map`: present ⇒ slot busy ⇒ `ResourceBusy` error (refuses to overwrite).
  - `unmap`, `vmem.rs` walks, `ensure_pt`: `!present` ⇒ no page table exists ⇒
    allocate / skip / error.
  - `identity_map.rs::verify_*`: compares `kernel_pde.is_present()` against
    `target_pde.is_present()` for structural equality of address spaces.
- Pure, read-only, total (`&self`, returns `bool`, no panic).
- **Callers don't care about:** any other flag, or how presence is stored.

### `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::is_present(&self)`
- **Only caller is internal** (`PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`). Expectation:
  returns `true` iff the `present` field equals `PresentFlag::Present` — i.e.
  exactly the `present` argument given to `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`.
- Pure, read-only, total.
- **Don't care about:** other flag fields.

### `PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address(&self)`
- **Callers assume:** returns the *physical base address* of the page frame the
  PDE points at, i.e. `frame_number << FRAME_SHIFT` (page-aligned). Concretely:
  - `ensure_pt`: when the PDE is already present, returns `pde.frame_address()`
    directly as the physical address of the existing page table.
  - `verify_kernel_mappings`: requires
    `kernel_pde.frame_address() == target_pde.frame_address()` for present
    entries to confirm two page directories share the same page tables.
- Pure, read-only, total; result is always frame-aligned (low `FRAME_SHIFT`
  bits are zero).
- **Callers don't care about:** the `FrameNumber` representation or shift
  details — only that the value is the byte address corresponding to the stored
  frame, and that it is the inverse of the `frame` passed to `new`.

## Abstract Resource

This module models a single **x86 32-bit Page Directory Entry**: a value that
binds a set of **paging control flags** to a **physical frame** (the page table,
or a large page, that the entry points to). From the caller's perspective a PDE
is `(present?, …other flags…, frame_address)` — an installable/decodable slot
in a page directory.

## Key Invariants (caller perspective)

# Caller Analysis: `x86/mem/paging/pde.rs` (Page Directory Entry)

## Script Output
See: `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-arch-x86-pde/find_callers_output.md`

> **Note on script results:** the LSP script reported **0 external callers** for
> every public function. This is a false negative: rust-analyzer indexed the
> `arch` crate in isolation and did not resolve cross-crate references from the
> `kernel` crate (and others). Manual `grep`/`view` across `src/` confirms there
> are many real callers, all of which live in the **`kernel`** crate. The
> analysis below is based on those verified call sites, not on the script's
> empty external-caller list.

## Scope

Verification-order target functions (only these are in scope):

- `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`
- `PageDirectoryEntry::new`
- `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`
- `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::is_present`
- `PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address`

## Where the callers live

| Caller file | Functions used |
|---|---|
| `src/kernel/src/hal/arch/shared/mem/mmu/page_directory.rs` | `PageDirectoryEntry::new`, `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`, `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`, (`from_raw_value`, `into_raw_value`, `frame_number`) |
| `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.rs` | `PageDirectoryEntry::new`, `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`, `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`, `PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address` |
| `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/vmem.rs` | `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present` (via `read_pde`) |
| `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs` | Verus `assume_specification[…]` for all in-scope functions |
| `src/uservm/src/guest_profiler/gva.rs` | `PageDirectoryEntry::SIZE` (const only — not in scope) |

`PageDirectoryEntryFlags::is_present` has **no direct external caller**; it is
reached only internally, through `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`, which
delegates `self.flags.is_present()`. It is in scope because its spec underpins
the spec of `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`.

## Verus Obligation (the primary consumer)

`src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs` declares external specifications
that the kernel's verified code depends on:

```rust
pub assume_specification[ PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new ]( … 8 flag args … ) -> PageDirectoryEntryFlags;
pub assume_specification[ PageDirectoryEntry::new ](flags: PageDirectoryEntryFlags, frame: FrameNumber) -> PageDirectoryEntry;
pub assume_specification[ PageDirectoryEntry::is_present ](pde: &PageDirectoryEntry) -> bool;
pub assume_specification[ PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address ](pde: &PageDirectoryEntry) -> usize;
```

The types are also lifted as opaque (`external_body`) spec types:
`ExPageDirectoryEntry`, `ExPageDirectoryEntryFlags`. This tells us the **View**
should expose the *abstract* properties these specs need (presence, frame
address, the flag values fed into `new`) — not the bit-level encoding.

## Caller Expectations

### `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new(present, read_write, user_supervisor, page_write_through, page_cache_disable, accessed, dirty, page_size)`
- **Callers assume:** the returned flags value faithfully *records each of the 8
  flag arguments*, so that a subsequent query reflects the inputs. In
  particular, callers that pass `PresentFlag::Present`/`NotPresent` expect
  `is_present()` on the resulting PDE to return `true`/`false` accordingly
  (see `page_directory.rs::map`/`unmap`, `identity_map.rs::ensure_pt`).
- It is a pure, total constructor — never fails, no side effects.
- **Callers don't care about:** the internal bit layout, field ordering, or how
  flags are packed into the raw `PteWord`.

### `PageDirectoryEntry::new(flags, frame)`
- **Callers assume:** the returned PDE pairs *these exact* `flags` with *this
  exact* `frame`. Specifically:
  - `is_present()` of the result == `flags.is_present()` (the present bit they
    passed in).
  - `frame_address()` of the result == `frame.into_raw_value() << FRAME_SHIFT`,
    i.e. the physical base address of `frame`.
- Pure, total constructor (no failure, no side effects).
- **Callers don't care about:** raw encoding; they immediately either store it
  via `write_pde`/`pd.write` (round-tripping through `into_raw_value`) or read
  it back through the accessors.

### `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present(&self)`
- **Callers assume:** returns the present bit exactly as set when the PDE was
  constructed / decoded. Used as a guard with strong control-flow meaning:
  - `map`: present ⇒ slot busy ⇒ `ResourceBusy` error (refuses to overwrite).
  - `unmap`, `vmem.rs` walks, `ensure_pt`: `!present` ⇒ no page table exists ⇒
    allocate / skip / error.
  - `identity_map.rs::verify_*`: compares `kernel_pde.is_present()` against
    `target_pde.is_present()` for structural equality of address spaces.
- Pure, read-only, total (`&self`, returns `bool`, no panic).
- **Callers don't care about:** any other flag, or how presence is stored.

### `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::is_present(&self)`
- **Only caller is internal** (`PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`). Expectation:
  returns `true` iff the `present` field equals `PresentFlag::Present` — i.e.
  exactly the `present` argument given to `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`.
- Pure, read-only, total.
- **Don't care about:** other flag fields.

### `PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address(&self)`
- **Callers assume:** returns the *physical base address* of the page frame the
  PDE points at, i.e. `frame_number << FRAME_SHIFT` (page-aligned). Concretely:
  - `ensure_pt`: when the PDE is already present, returns `pde.frame_address()`
    directly as the physical address of the existing page table.
  - `verify_kernel_mappings`: requires
    `kernel_pde.frame_address() == target_pde.frame_address()` for present
    entries to confirm two page directories share the same page tables.
- Pure, read-only, total; result is always frame-aligned (low `FRAME_SHIFT`
  bits are zero).
- **Callers don't care about:** the `FrameNumber` representation or shift
  details — only that the value is the byte address corresponding to the stored
  frame, and that it is the inverse of the `frame` passed to `new`.

## Abstract Resource

This module models a single **x86 32-bit Page Directory Entry**: a value that
binds a set of **paging control flags** to a **physical frame** (the page table,
or a large page, that the entry points to). From the caller's perspective a PDE
is `(present?, …other flags…, frame_address)` — an installable/decodable slot
in a page directory.

## Key Invariants (caller perspective)

1. **Constructor fidelity (flags):** for any flags `f = PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new(present, …)`,
   `f.is_present() == (present == Present)`.
2. **Constructor fidelity (entry):** for `e = PageDirectoryEntry::new(flags, frame)`,
   `e.is_present() == flags.is_present()` **and**
   `e.frame_address() == frame.into_raw_value() << FRAME_SHIFT`.
3. **Presence delegation:** `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present` ⟺
   `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::is_present` of its flags.
4. **Frame alignment:** `frame_address()` is always page-aligned (returns the
   physical base address of the frame; low `FRAME_SHIFT` bits are zero).
5. **Purity/totality:** `is_present` and `frame_address` are pure read-only
   queries; both `new` constructors are pure and total. None panic or mutate
   observable state.
6. **Encoding independence:** callers only ever observe a PDE through these
   accessors (and the `into_raw_value`/`from_raw_value` round-trip used by
   `read_pde`/`write_pde`); the concrete bit layout is not relied upon and may
   change without breaking callers, provided invariants 1–4 hold.

28. ( flags , frame )
29. ```

32. exactly two abstract facts in scope: **is it present?** and **what physical base
33. address does it point at?** (`frame << FRAME_SHIFT`).
34.

36. 
37. | Type | What it is to a caller |

39. | `PageDirectoryEntryFlags` | an immutable bundle of the eight paging control bits |
40. | `PageDirectoryEntry`      | the pair `(flags, frame)` |

43. immutable, `Copy`, pure-value tokens. Every in-scope function is either a pure
44. total constructor (`*::new`) or a pure read-only query (`is_present`,
45. `frame_address`); none mutate, allocate, fail, or panic.
46.

60. (the spec transitions in this document) **supersede** those placeholders without

62. `FrameNumber` abstraction (`frame@ : int`, bounded by `FrameNumber::spec_max()`)
63. and the frame/page size reuses the existing `mem::FRAME_SIZE` spec constant —
64. the same one `FrameNumber::spec_max()` is defined over — so the address

117.     pub frame: int,

121.     type V = PdeView;
122.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> PdeView;
123. }
124. ```

133.         true   // every combination of the eight bits is a legal flags value
134.     }
135. }

139. constructible by `new`, so its invariant is vacuous. (Kept explicit for
140. uniformity; it adds no obligation.)

145.         // The frame index is a valid frame number, so the derived physical base

 # View Design: `arch::x86::mem::paging::pde` (Page Directory Entry)
 
 In-scope (verification-order) targets — the **only** functions this View must
 serve, and the only ones any later phase may annotate:
 
 - `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`
 - `PageDirectoryEntry::new`
 - `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`
 - `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::is_present`
 - `PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address`
 
 All other items (`is_user`, `is_writable`, `is_large_page`, the `set_*`
 mutators, `from_raw_value`/`into_raw_value`, `flags`, `frame_number`, the `SIZE`
 const, the `TableEntry` impl, derived `Debug`/`Clone`/`Copy`) are **out of
 scope** and untouched. Where they are mentioned below it is only to confirm the
 View would *also* serve them without redesign.
 
 ---
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 This module models **one x86 32-bit page-directory entry**: a value that binds
 a set of **paging control flags** to a **physical frame** (the page table — or,
 for a large page, the mapped region — that the entry points at). To a caller a
 PDE is conceptually the pair
 
 ```
 ( flags , frame )
 ```
 
 an installable / decodable slot in a page directory. From it callers read back
 exactly two abstract facts in scope: **is it present?** and **what physical base
 address does it point at?** (`frame << FRAME_SHIFT`).
 
 Two types need abstraction, mirroring the source structure:
 
 | Type | What it is to a caller |
 |------|------------------------|
 | `PageDirectoryEntryFlags` | an immutable bundle of the eight paging control bits |
 | `PageDirectoryEntry`      | the pair `(flags, frame)` |
 
 It is *not* a collection, allocator, or state machine: both types are
 immutable, `Copy`, pure-value tokens. Every in-scope function is either a pure
 total constructor (`*::new`) or a pure read-only query (`is_present`,
 `frame_address`); none mutate, allocate, fail, or panic.
 
 ### Downstream contract this View must realize
 
 The verified kernel already pins the *external* contract of these types in
 `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs`:
 
 - the types are lifted opaque via `external_type_specification`
   (`ExPageDirectoryEntry`, `ExPageDirectoryEntryFlags`);
 - four **placeholder** `assume_specification`s (currently signature-only, no
   `ensures`) stand in for `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`,
   `PageDirectoryEntry::new`, `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present`,
   `PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address`.
 
 The View below is chosen so that, once `arch` is verified, the real `ensures`
 (the spec transitions in this document) **supersede** those placeholders without
 breaking kernel proofs. The frame index reuses the already-shipped
 `FrameNumber` abstraction (`frame@ : int`, bounded by `FrameNumber::spec_max()`)
 and the frame/page size reuses the existing `mem::FRAME_SIZE` spec constant —
 the same one `FrameNumber::spec_max()` is defined over — so the address
 `frame@ * FRAME_SIZE` is the inverse of the `frame` passed to `new`.
 
 ---
 
 ## View Types
 
 ### `PageDirectoryEntryFlags`
 
 The abstract value of a flags bundle is exactly its **eight boolean control
 bits**. Each source enum is two-valued (`0` = clear, `1 << SHIFT` = set), i.e.
 isomorphic to `bool`; the spec-world form of "the bit is set" is a `bool`.
 
 ```rust
 pub struct PdeFlagsView {
     /// Present (P) bit — the entry maps something.
     pub present: bool,
     /// Read/Write (R/W) bit — writes permitted (`is_writable`).
     pub writable: bool,
     /// User/Supervisor (U/S) bit — user-mode access permitted (`is_user`).
     pub user: bool,
     /// Page-Write-Through (PWT) bit.
     pub write_through: bool,
     /// Page-Cache-Disable (PCD) bit.
     pub cache_disabled: bool,
     /// Accessed (A) bit.
     pub accessed: bool,
     /// Dirty (D) bit.
     pub dirty: bool,
     /// Page-Size (PS) bit — entry maps a large page (`is_large_page`).
     pub large_page: bool,
 }
 
 impl View for PageDirectoryEntryFlags {
     type V = PdeFlagsView;
     // `closed`: callers reference `self@.present` etc., but the bit-packing into
     // the raw `PteWord` is hidden — exactly the encoding-independence the caller
     // analysis demands.
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> PdeFlagsView;
 }
 ```
 
 ### `PageDirectoryEntry`
 
 A PDE is the pair `(flags, frame)`. The frame is abstracted as its integer
 index (the `FrameNumber` View, `int`); the physical base address it yields is
 *derived* (`frame * FRAME_SIZE`), never stored.
 
 ```rust
 pub struct PdeView {
     /// The eight control bits this entry was built with.
     pub flags: PdeFlagsView,
     /// The frame index this entry points at (== the inner `FrameNumber`'s `@`).
     pub frame: int,
 }
 
 impl View for PageDirectoryEntry {
     type V = PdeView;
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> PdeView;
 }
 ```
 
 ---
 
 ## Well-formedness Invariants
 
 ```rust
 impl PageDirectoryEntryFlags {
     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
         true   // every combination of the eight bits is a legal flags value
     }
 }
 ```
 
 A flags bundle has no cross-field constraint: all 2⁸ combinations are
 constructible by `new`, so its invariant is vacuous. (Kept explicit for
 uniformity; it adds no obligation.)
 
 ```rust
 impl PageDirectoryEntry {
     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
         // The frame index is a valid frame number, so the derived physical base
         // address `frame * FRAME_SIZE` is well-defined and cannot overflow
         // `usize`. This is exactly the bound `FrameNumber` already guarantees;
         // restating it here lets `frame_address` be total with no `requires`.
         &&& 0 <= self.frame <= FrameNumber::spec_max()
         &&& self.flags.inv()
     }
 }
 ```
 
 The only real constraint is the frame bound, inherited verbatim from the
 `FrameNumber` type invariant. It is what makes `frame_address` total and
 overflow-free — the single guarantee the caller analysis pins on it.
 
 ---
 
 ## Spec Transition Functions
 
 Both types are immutable; the "transitions" relate constructor inputs / query
 self-state to the abstract result. They live on the View types (skill: reusable
 spec helpers belong on the View, not as extra `pub spec fn`s on the exec impl).
 
 ### Flag projection helper
 
 Each control enum is two-valued; project the "set" variant to `bool`:
 
 ```rust
 // One per flag enum, e.g.:
 pub open spec fn spec_present_set(p: PresentFlag) -> bool { p is Present }
 pub open spec fn spec_rw_set(f: ReadWriteFlag)      -> bool { f is ReadWrite }
 pub open spec fn spec_us_set(f: UserSupervisorFlag) -> bool { f is User }
 pub open spec fn spec_pwt_set(f: PageWriteThroughFlag) -> bool { f is WriteThrough }
 pub open spec fn spec_pcd_set(f: PageCacheDisableFlag) -> bool { f is CacheDisabled }
 pub open spec fn spec_a_set(f: AccessedFlag)        -> bool { f is Accessed }
 pub open spec fn spec_d_set(f: DirtyFlag)           -> bool { f is Dirty }
 pub open spec fn spec_ps_set(f: PageSizeFlag)       -> bool { f is Large }
 ```
 
 ### `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new(present, read_write, …, page_size)`
 
 Pure, total. Records each of the eight arguments faithfully (caller invariant 1):
 
 ```rust
 pub open spec fn spec_pde_flags_new(
     present: PresentFlag, read_write: ReadWriteFlag, user_supervisor: UserSupervisorFlag,
     page_write_through: PageWriteThroughFlag, page_cache_disable: PageCacheDisableFlag,
     accessed: AccessedFlag, dirty: DirtyFlag, page_size: PageSizeFlag,
 ) -> PdeFlagsView {
     PdeFlagsView {
         present:        spec_present_set(present),
         writable:       spec_rw_set(read_write),
         user:           spec_us_set(user_supervisor),
         write_through:  spec_pwt_set(page_write_through),
         cache_disabled: spec_pcd_set(page_cache_disable),
         accessed:       spec_a_set(accessed),
         dirty:          spec_d_set(dirty),
         large_page:     spec_ps_set(page_size),
     }
 }
 // new(..)  ensures  result@ == spec_pde_flags_new(present, …, page_size)
 ```
 
 ### `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::is_present(&self)`
 
 Pure read-only projection (caller invariant 3, the present field):
 
 ```rust
 // is_present(&self)  ensures  result == self@.present
 ```
 
 ### `PageDirectoryEntry::new(flags, frame)`
 
 Pure, total. Pairs *these exact* flags with *this exact* frame (caller invariant 2):
 
 ```rust
 pub open spec fn spec_pde_new(flags: PdeFlagsView, frame: int) -> PdeView {
     PdeView { flags, frame }
 }
 // new(flags, frame)  ensures  result@ == spec_pde_new(flags@, frame@)
 //                             (and result.inv(), since frame.inv() ⇒ frame@ ≤ MAX)
 ```
 
 From this single fact the caller's two derived expectations follow:
 `result.is_present() == flags.is_present()` and
 `result.frame_address() == frame@ * FRAME_SIZE`.
 
 ### `PageDirectoryEntry::is_present(&self)`
 
 Pure read-only; **delegates** to the flags' present bit (caller invariants 3
 and "presence delegation"):
 
 ```rust
 // is_present(&self)  ensures  result == self@.flags.present
 ```
 
 ### `PageDirectoryEntry::frame_address(&self)`
 
 Pure read-only; the physical base address of the pointed-at frame — the inverse
 of the `frame` given to `new`, always frame-aligned (caller invariant 4). `FRAME_SIZE`
 is the existing `mem::FRAME_SIZE` spec constant, `= 1 << FRAME_SHIFT`:
 
 ```rust
 // frame_address(&self)
 //   ensures  result as int == self@.frame * (mem::FRAME_SIZE as int)
 //            result as int % (mem::FRAME_SIZE as int) == 0          // frame-aligned (derived)
 ```
 
 The alignment clause is derivable from the product form and need not be a
 separate primitive guarantee; it is listed because `verify_kernel_mappings`
 compares frame addresses for present entries. Totality / no-overflow rests on
 `self.inv()` (`self@.frame ≤ FrameNumber::spec_max()`), so no `requires` is
 needed — matching the placeholder's contract-free signature.
 
 ---
 
 ## Design Rationale (per field — substitution test)
 
 > *If the implementation were completely rewritten with a different algorithm,
 > would this field still make sense?*
 
 | View element | Why it's needed | Substitution verdict |
 |--------------|-----------------|----------------------|
 | `PdeFlagsView.present` | The one bit every in-scope query observes; drives `is_present` on both types and the `map`/`unmap`/`ensure_pt` control flow (present ⇒ busy / table exists). | **Passes.** Any encoding still exposes a present bit. |
 | `PdeFlagsView.{writable, user, large_page}` | Recorded by `new` (constructor fidelity) and read by the sibling accessors `is_writable`/`is_user`/`is_large_page`; needed so `new`'s `ensures` rejects a buggy impl that drops an argument. | **Passes.** Each is a caller-visible paging permission/attribute, independent of bit layout. |
 | `PdeFlagsView.{write_through, cache_disabled, accessed, dirty}` | Recorded by `new`; complete the abstract "set of eight control bits" that the type *is*, so the constructor spec is total (no flag silently lost). | **Passes.** Architectural control bits, not impl artifacts. |

 | `PdeView.inv: frame ≤ FrameNumber::spec_max()` | Underwrites totality/overflow-safety of `frame_address` with no `requires`. | **Passes.** The bound is architectural (`MAX_ADDRESS/FRAME_SIZE`), not a code detail. |
 
 **Why eight booleans and not just `present`.** Minimality asks "is every field
 used in at least one in-scope spec?" — yes: all eight appear in
 `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`'s `ensures` (which *is* in scope). Dropping the
 other seven would make `new`'s spec one-sided (a buggy `new` that ignores

 both **complete** and **minimal**, and serves the out-of-scope accessors and
 later phases with no redesign.
 
 **Why `frame : int`, not the physical address.** The address is *derived*
 (`frame * FRAME_SIZE`); storing it would duplicate state and risk inconsistency
 between `is_present`/`frame_number`/`frame_address`. The index is the primitive
 that `new` consumes and `frame_address` reads — keep one, derive the other.
 `int` (not `usize`) keeps overflow out of specs; the bound lives in `inv()`.
 
 **Why composed (`PdeView` embeds `PdeFlagsView`), not flattened.** The source

 sibling and the standalone flags accessors.
 
 All view-design Step-4 checks pass — **Substitution** (table above),
 **Caller-only** (present + frame address + the eight bits are exactly the

 field used in an in-scope `ensures`), **No code-as-spec** (specs say *what* —
 "records each bit", "address = frame·FRAME_SIZE" — never *how* bits are packed).

 - **Flags View = single `present: bool`.** Rejected: makes
   `PageDirectoryEntryFlags::new`'s spec one-sided (cannot reject a `new` that
   mis-records the other seven arguments) and models only a sliver of the
   "page-directory-entry flags" resource. The other seven cost nothing in the

   constructor spec total and future-proof the sibling accessors.

   mathematical form and what `is_present` returns. (Pattern-matching is confined
   to the tiny projection helpers.)

   Rejected: `addr` is derived from `frame`; storing it duplicates state and

   independence, invariant 6), breaking the `into_raw_value`/`from_raw_value`

3. description: "Detect spec weakening via tree-sitter comparison against a baseline SHA. Use in specification, proving, and cheating-elimination phases to enforce that requires/ensures are never silently removed or relaxed."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Spec Drift Check
7. 
8. ## What Is Spec Drift?
9. 
10. Spec drift occurs when a function's `requires` or `ensures` clauses are removed,
11. relaxed, or replaced with weaker versions during a pipeline phase. This is a
12. critical integrity violation because:
13. 
14. - **Callers depend on the spec.** Upstream modules may have already proven their
15.   correctness assuming the original spec. Weakening it silently breaks those proofs.
16. - **Weakening is never acceptable as a proof strategy.** If a spec is hard to
17.   prove, the proof needs strengthening, not the spec weakening.
18. 
19. ## When to Use
20. 
21. Use this skill in **every review** during these phases:
22. - **Specification** — compare phase START baseline → current HEAD
23. - **Proving** — compare specification END → current HEAD
24. - **Cheating Elimination** — compare phase START baseline → current HEAD
25. 
26. ## How to Run
27. 
28. ### Auto-detect mode (recommended)
29. 
30. The `check` subcommand reads `pipeline_state.json` to automatically determine
31. the module, source file, current phase, and baseline SHA:
32. 
33. ```bash
34. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py check <module_name>
35. ```
36. 
37. ### Manual mode
38. 
39. Use `git-diff` when you need explicit control over the comparison range:
40. 
41. ```bash
42. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py git-diff <source_file> --before <baseline_sha> [--after <ref>]
43. ```
44. 
45. Where:
46. - `<source_file>` is the module's source file (relative to repo root)
47. - `<baseline_sha>` is the phase start SHA
48. - `--after` defaults to working tree if omitted
49. 
50. ### Exit Codes
51. - **0** — No contract drift detected ✅
52. - **1** — Contract drift detected ⚠ — spec weakening found
53. - **2** — Fatal error (tool failure)
54. 
55. ### Example
56. 
57. ```bash
58. # Auto-detect from pipeline state
59. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py check libhfs-src-internal-volume_impl
60. 
61. # Manual comparison between two SHAs
62. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py git-diff src/libs/slab/src/lib.rs \
63.     --before abc1234 --after def5678
64. ```
65. 
66. ## What Counts as Contract Drift
67. 
68. | Change | Verdict | Reason |
69. |--------|---------|--------|
70. | `ensures` clause removed | ⚠ FAIL | Callers may depend on it |
71. | `ensures` clause replaced with weaker version | ⚠ FAIL | Reduces verification value |
72. | `requires` clause added | ⚠ FAIL | Shifts proof burden to callers |
73. | `requires` clause strengthened | ⚠ FAIL | Callers may not satisfy it |
74. | Spec/proof function body changed | ⚠ FAIL | May change meaning of specs |
75. | Dependency spec fn body changed | ⚠ FAIL | Effective contract of callers changed |
76. | Top-level entry spec changed vs base branch | ⚠ HARD FAIL | Never allowed — verification target |
77. | Function with specs removed | ⚠ FAIL | Callers lose verified contract |
78. | `recommends` clause changed | ⚠ FAIL | May weaken soft preconditions |
79. | New `ensures` clause added | ✅ OK | Strengthens the contract |
80. | `requires` clause removed/relaxed | ✅ OK | Relaxes precondition for callers |
81. | Proof body changed (same spec) | ✅ OK | Only proof strategy changed |
82. 
83. ## Reviewer Checklist Item
84. 
85. When reviewing, verify:
86. 
87. 1. **Run the command.** Do not skip — check exit code.
88. 2. **If exit code 1:** Read the report. For each weakened function:
89.    - Is the original spec genuinely incorrect? If so, replace it with an
90.      equally strong (not weaker) correct spec.
91.    - Is this a proof difficulty workaround? **FAIL** — demand the
92.      original spec be restored and proven.
93. 3. **Document.** Record the drift check result in your review output.
94. 
95. ## Incorrect Spec vs Weakening
96. 
97. If a spec is genuinely wrong (e.g., encodes an incorrect formula or references
98. wrong fields), correct it. Note: if the code cannot satisfy a caller-required
99. spec, that is likely a **code bug**, not an incorrect spec. The correction must:
100. 1. Be equally strong — fix the error, do not weaken
101. 2. Still satisfy all caller expectations from `caller_analysis.md`
102. 
103. Weakening is **never** acceptable:
104. - "The proof is too hard" → strengthen the proof, not weaken the spec
105. - "Verus can't handle this" → use lemmas, external proof, or escalate
106. - "The caller doesn't actually need this" → the caller wrote their proof
107.   assuming the spec; removing it breaks their proof silently
108. 
109. ## Transitive Spec Drift
110. 
111. A function's effective contract includes the bodies of spec functions called
112. in its `requires`/`ensures`. The drift checker tracks these transitively
113. and flags `EFFECTIVE CONTRACT CHANGED` when a dependency spec fn
114. body is modified. Review these with the same rigor as direct clause changes.
115. 
116. ## Top-Level vs Internal Spec Drift
117. 
118. The pipeline distinguishes two levels of drift checking:
119. 
120. **Top-level entry point specs** are the functions listed in the verification
121. plan's `entries` field. These are always compared against the base branch.
122. Any change is a hard FAIL with no auto-fix.
123. 
124. **Internal module specs** are intermediate artifacts created to prove
125. top-level specs. The drift policy for internal specs:
126. 
127. - **Strengthening** (weaker precondition, stronger postcondition) is fine —
128.   this is normal refinement during proving.
129. - **Weakening** an existing spec may break callers further up the chain.
130.   If weakening is necessary, run a full `make verify` (not just the current
131.   module) to check that all callers still verify. If a caller breaks, adjust
132.   the caller to accommodate the change while still satisfying the top-level
133.   spec.
134.

1. ---
2. name: bug-reporting
3. description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Bug Reporting
7. 
8. Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
9. Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
10. to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.
11. 
12. ## Classification
13. 
14. After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
15. every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:
16. 
17. **True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
18. precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
19. logic error that always produces wrong results).
20. 
21. **Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
22. correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
23. a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
24. and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.
25. 
26. **False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
27. spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
28. limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).
29. 
30. ## When to Report
31. 
32. - **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
33. - **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
34.   needed and where they might come from.
35. - **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
36.   Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
37.   failure; see `verus-constraints`.
38. 
39. ## Auto-Fixable Bugs
40. 
41. Some true bugs are mechanical and can be fixed immediately to unblock
42. verification. **Fix these directly in the source code** and commit with
43. the `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix so the fix is clearly attributed to
44. verification. Still record them in `bugs.md`.
45. 
46. Auto-fixable categories:
47. - **Arithmetic overflow/underflow**: missing checked arithmetic or bounds
48.   checks (e.g. `a + b` → `a.checked_add(b)`, or adding a bounds guard)
49. - **Off-by-one**: fencepost errors in loop bounds or index calculations
50. - **Missing bounds check**: index used without prior length/capacity check
51. - **Unchecked cast**: lossy `as` cast without range validation
52. 
53. For each auto-fix:
54. 1. Make the **minimal** code change that fixes the bug
55. 2. Record the fix in `bugs.md` with full details (see Report Format)
56. 3. Add `// VERUS BUG FIX: <one-line description>` comment at the fix site
57. 4. Re-run AST consistency — the fix is a **pre-approved deviation** (bug fix category)
58. 5. Commit with `git commit --no-verify -m "[verus-ai] BUG FIX: <description>"` message
59.    (`--no-verify` is required because pre-commit hooks would reject exec changes)
60. 
61. Do NOT auto-fix:
62. - Algorithmic/design bugs (wrong data structure, incorrect state machine logic)
63. - Concurrency bugs (race conditions, missing synchronization)
64. - Anything requiring architectural changes
65. - Anything where the "fix" is unclear or has multiple valid approaches
66. 
67. For these, report only — a human should decide.
68. 
69. ## Report Format
70. 
71. Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
72. Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
73. and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.
74. 
75. ```markdown
76. ## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)
77. 
78. **What**: one-line summary of the issue.
79. **Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
80. **Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
81. verification command, and key error output.
82. **How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
83. be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
84. **Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
85. **Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
86. **Auto-Fixed**: Yes/No — if yes, describe the exact change made.
87. ```
88. 
89. If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.
90.

 the `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix so the fix is clearly attributed to
 verification. Still record them in `bugs.md`.
 
 Auto-fixable categories:
 - **Arithmetic overflow/underflow**: missing checked arithmetic or bounds
   checks (e.g. `a + b` → `a.checked_add(b)`, or adding a bounds guard)
 - **Off-by-one**: fencepost errors in loop bounds or index calculations
 - **Missing bounds check**: index used without prior length/capacity check
 - **Unchecked cast**: lossy `as` cast without range validation
 
 For each auto-fix:
 1. Make the **minimal** code change that fixes the bug
 2. Record the fix in `bugs.md` with full details (see Report Format)
 3. Add `// VERUS BUG FIX: <one-line description>` comment at the fix site
 4. Re-run AST consistency — the fix is a **pre-approved deviation** (bug fix category)
 5. Commit with `git commit --no-verify -m "[verus-ai] BUG FIX: <description>"` message
    (`--no-verify` is required because pre-commit hooks would reject exec changes)
 
 Do NOT auto-fix:
 - Algorithmic/design bugs (wrong data structure, incorrect state machine logic)
 - Concurrency bugs (race conditions, missing synchronization)
 - Anything requiring architectural changes
 - Anything where the "fix" is unclear or has multiple valid approaches
 
 For these, report only — a human should decide.
 
 ## Report Format
 
 Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
 Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
 and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.
 
 ```markdown
 ## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)
 
 **What**: one-line summary of the issue.
 **Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
 **Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
 verification command, and key error output.
 **How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
 be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
 **Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
 **Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
 **Auto-Fixed**: Yes/No — if yes, describe the exact change made.
 ```
 
 If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.

1. ---
2. name: spec-design
3. description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Spec Design Guide
7. 
8. ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
9. 
10. ### Qualities of a Good Spec
11. 
12. 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
13.    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
14.    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
15. 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
16.    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
17.    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
18.    verifies the copy, not the real code.
19. 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
20.    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
21.    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
22. 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
23.    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
24.    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
25. 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
26.    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
27.    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
28.    recursive spec functions.
29. 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
30.    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
31.    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
32.    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
33.    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
34. 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
35.    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
36.    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
37.    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
38.    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
39. 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
40.    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
41.    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
42.    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
43.    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
44.    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
45.    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
46.    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
47.    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
48.    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
49.    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
50. 
51. ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
52. 
53. If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
54. nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
55. spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
56. design model.
57. 
58. 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
59.    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
60.    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
61.    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
62.    annotation beats no annotation.
63. 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
64.    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
65.    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
66.    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
67.    Always search vstd first.
68. 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
69.    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
70.    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
71.    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
72.    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
73.    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
74.    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
75.    by vstd.
76.    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
77.    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
78.    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
79.    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
80. 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
81.    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
82. 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
83.    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
84.    make Verus pass.
85.    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
86.    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
87.    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.
88. 
89. ### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)
90. 
91. 1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or

 # Spec Design Guide
 
 ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
 
 ### Qualities of a Good Spec
 
 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
    verifies the copy, not the real code.
 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
    recursive spec functions.
 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
 
 ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
 
 If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
 nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
 spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
 design model.
 
 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
    annotation beats no annotation.
 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
    Always search vstd first.
 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
    by vstd.
    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
    make Verus pass.
    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.
 
 ### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)
 
 1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
    struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
    signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
    Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
    erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
    prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
    rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
    genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
    
    Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
    fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
 2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
    or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
    spec or proof instead.
    
    **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
    - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
      source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
      crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.
 
    **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**
 
    1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments

       Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
       requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).

       guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
       guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".

       clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
       callers will not check it.

       compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
       explicitly in the spec.

       the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
       code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"
    5. **Version sensitivity**: note the stdlib/crate version the
       assumption was checked against.
 
    - `external_body`: allowed on dependency functions in other modules as
      a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
      and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
      Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
      verification.
    
    `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
    See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
 3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
    the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
    loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
    it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
    or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
    must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
    implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
    strengthened later — that is expected.
 4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
    or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
    spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
 5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
    (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
 6. **Missing Frame Condition / Field-by-Field Conjunction** — ensures says
    what changed but not what didn't, OR lists unchanged fields one by one
    (fragile — easy to forget a field). **Always use struct update syntax**
    (`..old(self)@`) so completeness is guaranteed by construction:
 
    Bad (fragile — silent field omission):
    ```
    self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
    self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
    self@.field_c == new_value,
    // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
    ```
    Good (complete by construction):
    ```
    self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
    ```
    This applies everywhere state changes appear in ensures — whether
    inline or via spec transition functions.
 7. **Separate Ok/Err Conditions** — using `result.is_ok() ==> ...` and
    `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
    single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and
    prevents accidentally omitting one arm:
 
    Bad:
    ```
    ensures
        result.is_ok() ==> /* success postcondition */,
        result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,
    ```
    Good:
    ```
    ensures match result {
        Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
        Err(e) => self@ == old(self)@,
    }
    ```
 8. **Tautological Postconditions** — trivially true for any return value.
 9. **Subsumed Properties** — logically implied by a stronger property
    already present. Before adding an ensures clause, check: is this
    derivable from `self.inv()` combined with the other ensures? If so,
    delete it — redundant clauses obscure the spec's intent and make
    reviews harder.
 10. **Over-specification** — forcing a particular implementation strategy.
    Only add specificity when callers genuinely depend on it.
 11. **Scattered Invariant** — the same property appears in `requires` of
     every (or nearly every) method. A universally required property is an
     invariant — move it to `inv()` and maintain it in `ensures`.
 12. **`uninterp` as Verification Escape** — using `uninterp spec fn` to
     avoid writing a concrete spec definition, then injecting properties
     via `external_body` proof axioms. This combination is equivalent to
     `assume` — it introduces unverified assumptions about a function
     whose behavior is entirely under our control.
     `uninterp spec fn` is banned. All spec functions must have concrete
     definitions. If `uninterp` appears on `View::view()` of an
     `external_body` type, that is a mechanical consequence of the type

     as a separate `uninterp` allowance. If a spec function is hard to
     define concretely, that is a signal to simplify the abstraction,
     not to use `uninterp`.
 
 ### Error Path Spec Principles
 
 Every function that can fail should specify **what happens on failure**
 with the same rigor as the success path.
 
 1. **State Preservation** — on error, the state must not change.

name: spec-design
description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
   signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
   Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
   erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
   prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
   rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
   genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
   
   Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
   fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead.
   
   **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
   - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
     source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
     crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.

   **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**

   1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
      in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
      `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
      reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
      Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
      requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
   2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
      guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
      guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
      Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
      clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
      callers will not check it.
   3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
      compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
      explicitly in the spec.
   4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
      the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
      code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"
   5. **Version sensitivity**: note the stdlib/crate version the
      assumption was checked against.

   - `external_body`: allowed on dependency functions in other modules as
     a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
     and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
     Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
     verification.
   
   `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
   See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
   the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
   loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
   it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
   or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
   must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
   implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
   strengthened later — that is expected.
4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
   or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
   spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
   (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
6. **Missing Frame Condition / Field-by-Field Conjunction** — ensures says
   what changed but not what didn't, OR lists unchanged fields one by one
   (fragile — easy to forget a field). **Always use struct update syntax**
   (`..old(self)@`) so completeness is guaranteed by construction:

   Bad (fragile — silent field omission):
   ```
   self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
   self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
   self@.field_c == new_value,
   // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
   ```
   Good (complete by construction):
   ```
   self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
   ```
   This applies everywhere state changes appear in ensures — whether
   inline or via spec transition functions.
7. **Separate Ok/Err Conditions** — using `result.is_ok() ==> ...` and
   `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
   single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and

   Bad:

       result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,
